beats.trigger: ## Evaluations
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The Module 5 eval now runs on every output.
beats.got: Something called a judge scores things, a generator gets better, and I am not in it. I was not in Module 5 either.

beats.trigger: Start with the judge you saved at the close of Module 5.
beats.got: Homework. Nothing new.

beats.trigger: **Build** a self-improving eval loop: separate agents generate and judge, the Module 5 judge scores each round unchanged
beats.got: A learning-objectives list. 'Self-improving' makes me raise an eyebrow.

beats.trigger: Can agents improve if you define the outcome and let them find the path, or does organisational mess still matter too much?
beats.got: At least the question admits that organisational mess might win. I haven't heard that in a kickoff before.

beats.trigger: the system absorbs the catches without you.
beats.got: Without me. Marketing for the next steering group, that one.

beats.trigger: Humans will not cope with all the detail for long. You can stay inside one loop. You cannot stay inside all of them.
beats.got: True, and it matches how I run my own area. I read the summary and miss the detail.

beats.trigger: You saved the winner as `judges/groundedness-judge.md`: measured judgment, made runnable.
beats.got: A file that says what 'checked against the source' means, and a script runs it. A checklist that executes. OK.

beats.trigger: every name appears in the source, every number traces to a file, every claim cites evidence or admits the gap.
beats.got: Fabrication check. This is a real problem, and every manager who has read an AI summary knows it.

beats.trigger: Two mails both avoid overclaiming; one is forgettable, the other makes the reader act.
beats.got: Correct but useless is a different failure from invented, and you need a second check for it. Sensible, nothing exciting.

beats.trigger: If the judge moved, the score means nothing.
beats.got: Don't change the measure while you are measuring. I have watched KPIs get redefined mid-programme, so I understand this. It is also checkable by comparing the file's hash.

beats.trigger: The answer is never "the eval passed."
beats.got: Passing a test is not the same as being right. I knew that.

beats.trigger: Run at least three rounds, then continue until improvement stops.
beats.got: 45 minutes, and 30 of them are me walking away. I'd have taken the coffee anyway.

beats.trigger: Note what the judge catches; the tactic must learn that.
beats.got: Run it once by hand to see what it flags. A sensible first step.

beats.trigger: Now step away. Come back to a tactic tightened by a judge you did not move.
beats.got: A rules file rewritten between rounds while I'm gone. That is concrete, and it couldn't be done two years ago without a person doing every step.

beats.trigger: Failed numbers in round 3 mean the tactic cannot handle numbers yet; weak claims marked grounded mean the judge has a blind spot.
beats.got: It tells me what does not work yet, in plain words, and I can check the file hash myself. This is the first thing that sounded like it wasn't selling.

beats.trigger: And you weren't there.
beats.got: Each round feeds the next one's rules. The closing line is a bit theatrical.

beats.trigger: PDCA at the eval layer: Plan (generation tactic), Do (generate), Check (judge), Act (rewrite tactic).
beats.got: PDCA, with an AI label on it. That is the 2017 slide I expected, in one line.

beats.trigger: Convergence was the floor in Module 5. Eval-as-yardstick is the ceiling here.
beats.got: Reuse the loop with another judge. The floor and ceiling wording is getting repetitive.

beats.trigger: The judge had stopped finding things. That does not mean the work is done.
beats.got: A low flag count is not proof the work is good. They say so themselves, which I appreciate.

beats.trigger: A flat score is information about the judge, not the work.
beats.got: A green dashboard says the instrument is out of ideas, not that the work is good. I have lived this in three programmes.

beats.trigger: A generator that grades itself passes itself.
beats.got: Nobody has checked the checker. Score a handful by hand and compare, one afternoon per judge. That is a test I could actually run, and the first real advice so far.

beats.trigger: No release so far has told anyone what good means in your company.
beats.got: The part that stays with me is defining 'good' here. Fair point, though a bit pleased with itself.

beats.trigger: You move one level up: you design the loop and own the yardstick.
beats.got: A recap of the course so far, plus 'move up a level'. I have heard that line in every transformation.

beats.trigger: What would have to be true before you let the agent hit send?
beats.got: A five-item list of what must hold before a mail goes out. As a way to frame the decision it's workable.

beats.trigger: An ungrounded mail is a trust problem. A grounded but vague or tone-deaf mail is a usefulness problem.
beats.got: Nothing new. This is the floor and ceiling again.

beats.trigger: Variety in, selection out, memory keeps
beats.got: A slogan for generate, judge, save. It looks like a slide someone will want on the wall.

beats.trigger: Some categories never go without a human.
beats.got: There is a spectrum from draft only to auto-send, and some things never go automatic. That is a decision I would have to make, and I like that it admits the limit.

beats.trigger: Two judges now sit on disk: one keeps the work grounded, one steers it toward your standard.
beats.got: I write down what a good internal mail is for me and the agent turns it into a check. I would have to see it working.

beats.trigger: Every clean week is evidence the loop works, and each one erodes your ability to tell when the loop stops.
beats.got: The more the system works, the less I am able to notice when it breaks. That is the risk with every steering group, and this is the first time a training says it.

beats.trigger: If the answer is a month, put one in your calendar.
beats.got: Read one output start to finish like the recipient would. Cheap and sensible. It isn't news to anyone who has managed people.

beats.trigger: Your role in the loop is to design the conditions under which the system earns more autonomy, one loop at a time.
beats.got: The grand summary, with a diagram. Autonomy is 'earned', as if it were a probation review.

beats.trigger: The judge file stays untouched: that's the integrity of the loop.
beats.got: Ask the agent to tighten the rules file, leave the judge alone. Another prompt to paste.

beats.trigger: Which rule did you claim to remove but keep under another name? Quote both lines.
beats.got: A question I can ask when the summary sounds too kind. It treats the agent the way I treat a consultant's report. I like that.

beats.trigger: A flat score is information about the judge, not the work.
beats.got: Four lines. I would keep that one and maybe the one about the fixed judge.

beats.trigger: **Monday's first five agent calls, written down**
beats.got: Homework again, a list of five agent calls. I will think about it, not necessarily do it.

beats.trigger: Trust the loop you can inspect.
beats.got: A decent closing line. The first half just repeats the module.

take_homes: A green or flat score tells you about the instrument. Nobody has checked the checker, and you can do that in an afternoon by scoring a handful by hand and comparing.
If the thing is working, you stop reading it and lose the ability to see when it breaks. Read one output yourself, regularly.
Keep the judge fixed and check that with the file hash. Otherwise the improvement number means nothing.

monday.move: Nothing new on the loop. One small test: take five of the AI-written summaries my team already uses, score them by hand against what I know, and see whether I would have sent them back.
monday.who: Me, with one analyst from my team to read them blind.
monday.when: One afternoon sometime this month, if the calendar allows.
monday.stop_condition: If I would have passed nearly all five, I drop it. If I would have sent several back, I take that to the programme owner.
monday.blocker: Steering groups from the last programme, and the fact that I have not built any of this myself.

misconception.why: The module never argues that this isn't another wave, so 'wait and see' stands. What I noticed is that this is the first material that said what does not work yet (blind spots, a flat score meaning little, the human losing the eye). That makes me more willing to run one small test, but it doesn't change my view that it may blow over. The PDCA and 'move one level up' bits sounded like the last three programmes.

one_line: Mostly the usual deck with AI on it, but the bit about nobody checking the judge, and the warning that the better it works the less you'll notice when it breaks, are worth an afternoon.
